title: Trump Administration Proposes Raising H-1B Wage Floors by Up to 33 Percent
excerpt: The Department of Labor's proposed rule would significantly increase prevailing wage requirements for H-1B workers and green card applicants, adding to a series of measures reshaping skilled immigration.
body:
The Trump administration has moved to sharply raise the minimum salaries U.S. employers must pay foreign workers on H-1B visas and several other visa categories, in its latest effort to discourage companies from hiring lower-paid immigrants over American workers.

The Department of Labor published the proposed rule in the Federal Register on March 27, 2026, targeting the prevailing wage methodology that has been in place since 2005. Pay floors for H-1B workers would rise between 21% and 33% depending on experience level, according to the Wall Street Journal.

"This proposed rule will help ensure that employers pay foreign workers wages that reflect the real market value of their labor, in addition to protecting the wages and job opportunities of American workers."

— Lori Chavez-DeRemer, U.S. Secretary of Labor

How the Wage Levels Would Change

The DOL classifies positions into four wage tiers based on job duties and required experience, using Bureau of Labor Statistics survey data. Under the proposed rule, Level I wages for entry-level workers would jump from the 17th percentile to the 34th percentile of the occupational wage distribution. Level II would rise from the 34th to the 52nd, Level III from the 50th to the 70th, and Level IV from the 67th to the 88th, according to Bloomberg Law.

"And on July 17, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security ended "duration of status" for international students, a move the Brookings Institution estimated could cost the U.S."

For entry-level workers, that translates to an 18% increase over average offered wages between 2020 and 2024, the DOL projects. Across all levels, the average certified wage would rise by approximately $14,000 per year per sponsored employee, according to analysis by the law firm Duane Morris.

The rule also covers the permanent labor certification process for EB-2 and EB-3 immigrant visas. More than 57% of PERM applications in fiscal year 2024 were filed on behalf of employees already on H-1B status, the DOL noted, making these programs deeply interlinked.

Part of a Sweeping Immigration Overhaul

The wage rule is one piece of a broader campaign to reshape skilled immigration. The White House imposed a $100,000 fee for new H-1B petitions in September 2025. The FY2027 H-1B lottery introduced a wage-weighted selection process, favoring higher-paid positions—USCIS data showed 71.5% of selected beneficiaries held a U.S. advanced degree, up from 57% a year earlier. And on July 17, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security ended "duration of status" for international students, a move the Brookings Institution estimated could cost the U.S. economy $72 billion to $145 billion over a decade.

Impact on Indian Professionals

Indian nationals form the largest group of H-1B beneficiaries and account for a significant share of EB-2 and EB-3 green card applicants. The proposed wage increases would hit entry-level and early-career workers hardest—the segment that includes many recent graduates from U.S. universities seeking to transition from student visas to H-1B status.

"There's little evidence of a pay disparity in studies comparing workers with the same levels of education and experience."

— Stuart Anderson, Executive Director, National Foundation for American Policy

A George Mason University study found H-1B holders actually earn salaries up to 6% higher than comparable U.S. professionals. The Penn Wharton Budget Model projected that the wage-weighted lottery alone would increase average compensation of selected registrants by about 10%, and the proposed wage rule would compound that shift by reclassifying many positions into higher tiers.

What Happens Next

The 60-day comment period closed May 26, 2026, drawing extensive feedback from employers, immigration attorneys, and universities. The DOL must now review comments before publishing a final rule, a process that typically takes several months. If finalized, the rule would take effect 30 to 60 days after publication.

Legal challenges are widely expected. A similar rule proposed during Trump's first term in October 2020 was vacated by a federal court before it took effect. The current proposal has drawn criticism from researchers who argue the DOL manufactured a wage gap to justify the increases. Immigration attorneys recommend that companies with pending PERM cases or upcoming H-1B extensions review their wage levels now to prepare.
